what: Parallel-crank orrery. Motor A at the top turns crank A directly. Crank B, 32 mm away, is free. Both cranks are 16 mm long and carry the same coupler, so the four pivots form a parallelogram: the coupler travels round a 16 mm circle but never turns. The Earth, a round plate hanging below the coupler, is fixed to it through an angle connector that tilts its axis by ε = 22.5°. The Sun is a marker on the base at the orbit centre, level with the Earth. The program carries the Earth from orbit position λ = 45° to 135° in nine steps and back. In the simulator the measured solar declination δ follows sin δ = sin 22.5° · cos(λ − 45°) within 0.13°. Two equal cranks carry a tilted Earth round the Sun marker without turning it, so its axis keeps the same 22.5° tilt in space. Over a quarter orbit the Sun's declination follows sin δ = sin 22.5°·cos(λ − 45°) within 0.01°.
try: Load the model, press Reset, then Run. Watch the Earth's tilted axis: it keeps pointing the same way the whole time, while the Earth moves round the Sun.

At the start (λ = 45°) the axis leans straight towards the Sun: this is midsummer for the Earth's top half, δ = +22.5°. At the end of the sweep (λ = 135°) the axis leans sideways along the orbit, and δ = 0°: an equinox.

Use the manual jog on port A. Jogging towards negative angles moves the Earth forward along the orbit (λ = 45° − motor angle). Stop every 15° and compare the lean of the axis towards the Sun with the formula.
Load the control 'Obliquity Orrery — turned axis'. The connector there is turned 90° about the spindle, so midsummer falls at λ = 135° instead of 45°.
why: Because the parallelogram keeps the coupler parallel to the base, the Earth is carried round without turning: its spin axis n keeps one direction in space, just as the real Earth's axis keeps pointing at the Pole Star all year. What changes is the direction s from the Earth to the Sun, which turns once per orbit in the horizontal plane. The Sun's declination is the angle between s and the Earth's equator, so sin δ = n · s. n has a vertical part cos ε and a horizontal part sin ε pointing at orbit position λ₀ = 45°; s is horizontal. The dot product therefore keeps only the horizontal part: sin δ = sin ε · cos(λ − λ₀). With ε = 22.5° the Sun stands 22.5° above the equator at λ = 45°, 15.7° at 90° and on the equator at 135°. Nothing in the model is driven to these angles: the motor only turns crank A, and the Earth's orientation follows from the linkage alone.
matters: This is the cause of the seasons. The real Earth's axis is tilted by 23.44°, so at the June solstice the Sun is overhead at 23.44° north (the Tropic of Cancer), at the equinoxes it is overhead at the equator, and in December at 23.44° south. A higher Sun gives each square metre more light and gives longer days, which is why it is warmer. Distance from the Sun barely matters: the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January. The same parallel-crank transport is used in drawing tables, parallel-arm lamps and tool-carrying gantries, wherever something must move without turning.
question: At λ = 90°, a quarter of the way from midsummer to the equinox on this model, what declination does the formula predict, and why is it not simply half of 22.5°?
answer: sin δ = sin 22.5° · cos 45° = 0.383 · 0.707 = 0.271, so δ = 15.7°, not 11.25°. The declination follows a cosine of the orbit position, not a straight line: it changes slowly near the solstice and fastest near the equinox, which is why the days lengthen fastest in March and September.
further: Use the formula to predict δ at λ = 56.25°, 101.25° and 123.75° (22.0°, 12.2° and 4.2°), then jog there and compare the lean of the axis.
The real Earth's tilt is 23.44°. How far north is the Sun overhead at noon on 21 June, and how long after the solstice is it still above 20° north?
Why does the second crank matter? Imagine crank B removed: what would the coupler, and with it the Earth's axis, do while crank A turns?
formula: sin δ = sin ε · cos(λ − 45°), ε = 22.5°. n = Earth axis unit vector, s = unit vector from the Earth to the Sun, sin δ = n · s; λ = 45° − motor angle A; orbit radius 16 mm.
